title: Imaging Degradation of III-V Quantum Dots Using Liquid-Phase TEM
content: Semiconductor quantum dots (QDs) are inherently less stable than bulk materials due to their high surface-to-volume ratio, making them susceptible to decomposition in the presence of water and oxygen in practical applications. Understanding the degradation mechanisms of semiconductor nanocrystals, particularly focusing on the pathways of structural transformation during degradation, facilitates the development of stable nanocrystals with resilient structures, which further significantly impacts their photophysical properties [1]. Meanwhile, environmentally benign and non-toxic III-V materials such as InP-based QDs have been less studied [2-4]. This calls for not only observations on their morphological change during degradation, but also their structural evolution embedded in the native environment. In-situ liquid-phase transmission electron microscopy (TEM) enables direct observations of nanocrystal transformations especially their degradation in real time and real space in native environment, where the reactions are controlled based on electron beam [5, 6]. Complementarily, the recently emergent four-dimensional scanning transmission electron microscopy (4D-STEM) utilizes a nm-sized probe to raster scan a region of interest (ROI) and to collect electron diffraction patterns (DPs), from which the crystal identity, crystal orientation, extent of disorder, and strain can be mapped at nm resolution [7]. Conducting 4D-STEM the native liquid has been challenging. On one hand, electron signal decays fast in the thick liquid layer, leading to a low signal-to-noise ratio; on the other, the electron beam radiation needs to be controlled to ensure the stability of the native environment by low-dose imaging, making the signal-to-noise ratio even worse.
